3 signs your AI costs are getting out of hand | AX1S Infra
AI costs scale with users, not with infrastructure
AI costs behave differently from a regular cloud bill. They don't scale with your infrastructure, but with your users. And users simply grow faster than budgets are adjusted.
These are three signs we encounter most often at organisations where the AI bill has already got out of hand, or is about to in the short term.
1. Nobody can answer the question "what does our AI feature cost per user?"

If that question gets a shrug, that is itself the signal. A team building a chatbot or recommendation engine looks at functionality. Nobody calculates by default what each extra user adds in inference costs. At AX1S we see this in almost every intake conversation: the technology works, adoption grows, but the cost per user has never been calculated. With the {1}AI Cost Calculator{/1} you can work it out in a few minutes, including the growth projection.
2. The monthly invoice structurally deviates from the previous one, for no clear reason

With regular cloud costs, an increase can usually be traced to a concrete cause: new capacity, a new project. With AI costs that clear trigger is often missing. The invoice simply rises with usage, and nobody has actively tracked that usage. Anyone who has seen this pattern for a few months without an explanation is almost certainly behind the facts.
3. Success first feels like a compliment, and only later like a bill

An AI feature takes off. Users find it valuable, adoption grows, everyone is happy. That very success is what lets the costs quietly grow along, without anyone consciously looking at it. By the time the invoice stands out, the growth is long under way. Not because something went wrong, but because nobody associates success with a rising cost item.
None of these three signs is a problem on its own. The problem arises when nobody recognises them before the bill comes in at three times what was expected.

This AI project looked cheap, until the bill arrived | AX1S Infra
Month 1: a small pilot
A team gets the green light for a pilot: an AI model that answers customer questions automatically. Test budget: small. Scope: a hundred conversations a day, purely for validation.

The results are good. Customers respond positively, the team is enthusiastic, and the pilot's costs barely stand out in the monthly invoice. Everyone is happy. The idea is approved for roll-out to the entire customer service department.
Month 2: roll-out without recalculation
The model goes live for all incoming conversations. Nobody recalculates upfront what that means; the pilot worked well, so why would scaling up be any different from more of the same?
The number of conversations rises from a hundred to ten thousand a day. Not gradually, but immediately, because that was the whole point of the roll-out.
Month 3: the bill

The first full invoice comes in. Nobody had a number in mind to compare it against, so at first the amount doesn't even stand out. Only when finance puts it next to the previous month does it become clear: the costs are not a hundred times, but almost three hundred times higher than during the pilot.
Only then does the reason become visible. The pilot ran on a test environment with a different pricing model. Production has different rates, and nobody had calculated that difference upfront.

The model still works well. Customers are still satisfied. But the cost per conversation turns out to be three times higher than the business case had foreseen, and that difference could have been calculated from day one, if someone had asked.

The lesson isn't in the technology, but in the order. A pilot proves that something works. A calculation at full scale proves that it stays profitable. Those are two different questions, and usually only the first one is asked.

Oh no, the budget has been exceeded again | AX1S Infra
A reasonable estimate, on paper
At the start of the quarter the cloud budget is set. An amount based on the usage of the previous months, plus a margin for growth. On paper a reasonable estimate.

Halfway through the quarter a new feature goes live. Not planned as a big expense, more as a logical next step on the roadmap. Nobody links that go-live back to the budget, because the feature itself costs "almost nothing" to build.
What nobody calculates

What nobody calculates is what the feature costs to run. The new functionality makes many calls to an external AI model, and every call counts towards the bill. In the first weeks that barely stands out; usage is still low while users discover the feature.
Then adoption increases. Exactly as hoped, which makes it hard to see as a problem. More users, more calls, more costs, all in the same direction as the success of the feature itself.
Towards the end of the quarter

Towards the end of the quarter the budget has not been slightly exceeded, but by tens of percent. Nobody saw it coming, because nobody had ever linked the new feature to the existing budget. The budget was based on the past, and the feature changed the future without anyone adjusting the amount.

In hindsight the question is easy to ask: why wasn't this spotted earlier? The answer is almost always the same. There was no interim moment when anyone put current usage next to the budget. The only check was the report at the end of the quarter, and by then it was too late to adjust.
An overrun is rarely the result of one big miss. Usually it is the sum of small, individually logical decisions that were never fed back to the whole.

The FinOps maturity model | AX1S Infra
The FinOps maturity model: where does your organisation stand?
Crawl, walk, run

FinOps is not a project with an end date, but a growth path. The FinOps Foundation describes this path in three phases: Crawl, Walk and Run, where each phase represents a deeper level of cost awareness, automation and collaboration between engineering, finance and business. Most organisations underestimate which phase they are actually in, and that is exactly where savings opportunities remain.
Crawl: visibility as the starting point

In this phase cost data is fragmented, consistent tagging is missing and cost control is reactive, usually only when the invoice arrives. Recognisable by loose spreadsheets, a single dashboard nobody consults structurally, and surprise afterwards at spikes in usage. This is nothing to be ashamed of: almost every organisation starts here.
Walk: from reactive to proactive

Here structure emerges: consistent tagging, recurring cost reports per team, and the first steps towards rightsizing and commitment discounts. Teams start to weigh costs in technical decisions, and there is usually a designated owner (or small team) for FinOps within the organisation.
Run: costs as a continuous part of engineering

In the most mature phase cost awareness is woven into the way of working: automated anomaly detection, cost allocation that directly influences teams, and architectural decisions that take cost-effectiveness into account right from the drawing board. Saving is then no longer an action, but a property of the system.
{1} Crawl: cost data is visible, but fragmented and reactive
{1} Walk: structural reporting, first optimisations, clear ownership
{1} Run: automated, proactive, embedded in engineering culture

Important: you don't have to be in the same phase for every practice (cost allocation, optimisation, planning). Most organisations, for example, are far along in visibility but still early in automated optimisation.
Why this classification is practically useful

The model prevents you from reaching for advanced automation too quickly while the basics (consistent tagging, shared ownership, reliable reporting) are still missing. Conversely, it also prevents mature organisations from getting stuck in manual processes that could have been automated long ago.
The first step is simple: map out which phase you are actually in per practice, instead of going on a feeling. That starting point immediately determines which interventions deliver the most.

Wait, is this investment still profitable? | AX1S Infra
Eighteen months ago, a clear business case

Eighteen months ago an AI model went live that analyses customer data to make personalised recommendations. The business case was clear: higher conversion, satisfied customers, an investment that would pay for itself within a year.

The model is still running. The recommendations work, customers respond positively, and nobody has had reason to doubt it. That is exactly the problem: because it functions well, nobody has ever revisited the original calculation.
What has changed in the meantime

A lot has changed in the meantime. The customer base has grown, which means the model is called more often than at the start. Provider prices have risen slightly. And the conversion improvement the model was supposed to deliver has not been measured separately since the first months after go-live.

When someone finally takes the plunge and redoes the calculation, the picture turns out different from expected. The costs, through growth and price rises combined, have almost doubled compared with the original estimate. The return has never been re-measured, so nobody can say with certainty whether it has grown along.

The model isn't necessarily a bad investment. But nobody can currently say out loud whether that is still true, and that is a different problem from a bad business case: it is a business case that has never been tested again.

That is a pattern that occurs more often than you'd think. An investment is approved based on a calculation at one point in time, and then keeps running indefinitely without anyone repeating that calculation.

Oh no, nobody ever checked this cost item | AX1S Infra
Two years ago a logical choice

Two years ago a reserved instance was purchased. At the time a logical choice: the team knew exactly what would be running, the discount was attractive, and the commitment seemed a sensible investment.

A lot has changed since. A migration to a new architecture, a team that was split up, a product that was developed further. Nobody ever checked whether that old commitment still fits what is actually running now.
Stable, until someone asks
The amount still sits neatly in the monthly report. Unchanged, quarter after quarter. To anyone glancing at it, that looks reassuring: stable, predictable, no surprises.

Until someone, during a scan, asks the question nobody had asked any more: what is this actually still running on? The answer takes longer than expected. The person who made the original choice no longer works there. The underlying documentation can't be found. And when usage is finally laid next to it, the commitment turns out to be utilised for only a fraction.
For two years, capacity has been paid for that largely went unused, not because anyone was negligent, but because nobody ever asked the question the scan now did.
That is the pattern behind most outdated cost items. Not one big mistake, but the simple fact that nobody looked at it any more once the amount felt "normal".
